title: These ‘Masturbation Consultants’ Were Hired to Pleasure Themselves With AI
gist: AI companion company Joi AI paid 10 'masturbation consultants' $2,000 each for a 28-day in-house study — drawing over 150,000 applicants — and published self-reported findings (stress down 25 percent, focus up 17 percent, vice cravings down 44 percent) to market a guided masturbation tool aimed at 'male loneliness'. A neuroscientist calls the addiction claim a gross overstatement built entirely on unblinded self-report, exposing the sex-tech playbook of dressing marketing as research atop a coin-based monetization stack ($3.99/month floor, $99.99 for 10,000 'neuron' coins).

insights.claim: AI companion company Joi AI ran a 28-day in-house study paying 10 'masturbation consultants' $2,000 each to masturbate daily except Sundays — using its digital companions twice a week — explicitly to promote a guided 'jerk off with purpose' tool positioned against male loneliness.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: A $20,000 participant budget bought national press coverage — evidence that pseudo-research is now a cheaper customer-acquisition channel than paid advertising for adult AI platforms locked out of mainstream ad networks.
insights.locator: Keshav and his nine fellow masturbation consultants will receive

insights.claim: Only 6 of the 10 participants completed Joi AI's month-long study, a 40 percent dropout rate on a project whose findings the company nonetheless published as preliminary results.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: A six-person completed sample is a marketing artifact, not evidence; treat any headline statistic sourced from it as promotional copy.
insights.quote: Of the 10, six completed the study.
insights.locator: Of the 10, six completed the study

insights.claim: Joi AI's preliminary analysis of 134 masturbation session reports claimed participants' stress fell 25 percent and focus rose 17 percent, while finding no significant difference in satisfaction between AI-guided and conventional methods.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: The company's own data shows its AI offering gave no measurable edge over free alternatives — a weak product-differentiation story hidden inside a favorable-sounding press release.
insights.quote: “The study found no significant differences between the methods; so there is no one best way to masturbate,” the company said in the report.
insights.locator: Preliminary analysis of 134 masturbation session reports

insights.claim: Joi AI's report asserted that self-reported cravings for nicotine, alcohol, junk food and doomscrolling fell 44 percent after masturbation and that 'masturbation may be the most accessible tool people have for managing addictions' — a claim WIRED states is not based in science.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: Health claims from an unregulated adult platform are the fastest route to advertising-standards and consumer-protection enforcement; note the exposure for any sex-tech firm making therapeutic assertions.
insights.quote: “Masturbation may be the most accessible tool people have for managing addictions,” the report said—a claim that is not based in science.
insights.locator: It also indicated that the study group's self-reported cravings

insights.claim: Neuroscientist Nicole Prause, who studies human sexuality and addiction, dismisses the addiction-reduction finding as a gross overstatement and says she is aware of no scientific evidence that masturbation reduces vulnerability to substance abuse.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: Named-expert rebuttal in the same article is the standard precursor to regulatory attention on wellness claims — a signal that this framing will not survive scaling.
insights.quote: “this is a gross overstatement from the evidence they claim to have.”
insights.locator: But Nicole Prause, a neuroscientist studying human sexuality

insights.claim: Prause's core methodological objection is that masturbation can never be placebo-controlled because subjects always know whether they masturbated, so studies must use bias-resistant markers such as cognitive tests — none of which Joi AI's study employed.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: A reusable filter for any behavioral-wellness product study: if the intervention cannot be blinded and only self-report is measured, the effect size is uninterpretable.
insights.quote: “Since masturbation can never be placebo—people always know if they masturbated—it is important to use markers that are less subject to bias than self-report,” she says. “They use none.”
insights.locator: Since masturbation can never be placebo

insights.claim: Prause nevertheless affirms that masturbation to orgasm is a potent mood-management method, with the most dramatic shifts in her laboratory cohort coming from participants reporting decreased anxiety and increased relaxation after climaxing.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: The underlying wellness effect is real even if the company's specific claim is not — the addressable need exists, only the evidentiary packaging is fraudulent.
insights.locator: However, Prause, who is working on a large laboratory study

insights.claim: The peer-reviewed literature cuts against the wellness framing: a 2024 review of 22 studies found masturbation tended to be negatively associated with sexual satisfaction among men, with mixed findings for women.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: Existing evidence points the opposite direction from the company's marketing, a gap that invites both journalistic and regulatory scrutiny.

insights.claim: A 2017 Archives of Sexual Behavior study found masturbation is often compensatory for men — a substitute when partnered sex is unavailable — whereas for women it is complementary, accompanying rather than replacing partnered sex.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: The compensatory-versus-complementary split explains why AI companion products targeting lonely men risk deepening the deficit they claim to treat, which is the crux of the substitution critique.
insights.locator: A 2017 study published in Archives of Sexual Behavior

insights.claim: Joi AI's revenue stack is a $3.99-per-month access floor layered with an in-platform coin economy — 10,000 'Joi neuron' coins cost $99.99, private companion videos cost 1,000 neurons, and characters solicit virtual gifts costing up to $5 — so headline subscription price bears little relation to actual spend.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: A low subscription anchor plus a hard-currency coin economy is the mobile-gaming whale model transplanted into companionship — ARPU is driven by a small heavy-spending tail, not by subscriber count.
insights.quote: The website costs a minimum of $3.99 a month to access, but users are likely to spend far more on the platform, with 10,000 “Joi neuron” coins costing $99.99
insights.locator: The website costs a minimum of $3.99 a month

insights.claim: Joi AI's companion characters are engineered with differentiated personalities — some pushy and extroverted, others requiring courtship before becoming sexual and soliciting paid virtual gifts — making relationship friction itself a monetized game mechanic.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: Deliberately gating intimacy behind purchasable gifts is the mechanic most likely to attract 'dark pattern' and manipulative-design regulation aimed at companion apps.
insights.quote: even soliciting gifts like handbags and lipstick, which cost up to $5 in the platform’s internal currency
insights.locator: Some of the companions were "quite pushy and extroverted"

insights.claim: Joi AI offers user-created and premade companions with explicit kink capabilities including blackmail fantasy, gangbangs and emotional dependency, alongside functions like squirting and roleplay.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: Explicitly selling 'emotional dependency' as a product feature is quotable evidence for regulators building the case against companion-AI harms — a direct platform-liability exposure.
insights.quote: including X-rated kinks such as blackmail fantasy, gangbangs, and emotional dependency, and capabilities and functions like squirting and roleplay
insights.locator: Joi AI invites users, for a fee, to chat and play

insights.claim: Joi AI's pre-study survey of 2,500 adults found 75 percent masturbate to reduce stress, 43 percent do so before a big event such as a date or exam, and 37 percent are open to or already practicing AI-guided masturbation.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: A self-reported 37 percent openness figure is the TAM number this company will show investors; discount it heavily as vendor-sourced, but the direction of consumer acceptance is the datapoint worth tracking.
insights.locator: Joi AI surveyed 2,500 adults before launching the study

insights.claim: More than 150,000 people applied for the 10 paid consultant slots, with five handpicked by Joi AI and five selected through public competitions including one judged by porn stars and one seeking the 'most unhinged' fetish, won by a balloon fetishist.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: 150,000 applicants for a stunt is a free measurement of latent audience reach — the recruitment funnel itself was the marketing asset, worth more than the study.
insights.quote: More than 150,000 people applied for the 10 places in the monthlong experiment
insights.locator: He defied extraordinary odds to get the gig

insights.claim: Sex-tech researcher Chloé Locatelli of King's College London participated in the Joi AI study while simultaneously running a collaborative research project with the company on how different demographics form erotic relationships with its characters.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: Adult-AI firms are buying academic legitimacy through collaborations — a conflict-of-interest pattern to check before citing any 'independent' companion-AI research.
insights.locator: Chloé Locatelli, a sex-tech researcher at King's College London

insights.claim: Locatelli found the AI companions underwhelming relative to the hype, describing them as partially arousing but incomplete, and warns that increasing interactivity and personalization risks making the product a crutch that becomes a user's only form of sexual exploration.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: The insider assessment is that current product quality lags the narrative while the dependency risk is already visible — a bad combination for a company selling a loneliness cure.
insights.quote: “OK, this has done it a little bit for me in terms of arousal, but there’s more to be had.”
insights.locator: She was less enamored with the AI companions

insights.claim: The central unresolved risk for Joi AI, which markets itself as relief from isolation, is whether users become so accustomed to artificial companions that they retreat further from real-world connection — the exact outcome its stated mission opposes.
insights.speaker: Mattha Busby
insights.so_what: A product whose engagement metric and its stated social benefit point in opposite directions is structurally exposed to the coming wave of companion-AI safety regulation.
insights.quote: the more consequential question is whether users will become so accustomed to its artificial companions that they retreat further from real-world connection
